sections.heading: Owning how I have failed you
sections.text: Mighty God, I come to you without excuses. You have given me gifts, time, chances to serve, and words that could have helped others, and I have often used them poorly or not at all. I have spoken carelessly, made promises I did not keep, served you half-heartedly, drifted backward when I should have followed, and let useless, proud, and selfish thoughts take up space in my heart. I repent of these sins and of the foolishness underneath them.
theological_themes: Confession of misused gifts, neglected opportunities, careless speech, unfaithful service, and inward sin before a holy God.
Repentance that does not excuse or minimize personal responsibility.

scripture_references.connection: James treats speech as a serious test of the heart and warns that words can do real harm. This supports the prayer’s confession of careless and ill-advised words as sin, not merely social awkwardness.
John calls believers to honest confession rather than denial, with confidence in God’s faithful forgiveness. The section follows that pattern by naming sin plainly before God.

sections.heading: Asking you to cover my sin and heal what I have damaged
sections.text: Please cover my guilt through the blood of Jesus. Let my sin be swallowed up in his mercy, and do not let my impatience, pettiness, sharpness, or ugly behavior keep spreading damage. Where I have wounded someone by being unkind, comfort and restore them in ways I cannot. Where I have turned away from need, sorrow, or poverty, have mercy on me. Do not treat me as I have treated others. Keep your heart open to my need, even when I have closed mine to people who needed me.
theological_themes: A plea for God to restrain the harmful consequences of sin and to show mercy where the person has failed to show mercy.
Awareness that sins against God often wound other people.

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds forgiveness in redemption through Christ’s blood, making it fitting to ask God to deal with guilt through Jesus rather than through personal merit.
Jesus connects receiving mercy from the Father with extending mercy to others. This directly illuminates the prayer’s concern over having withheld compassion while still needing God’s mercy.
God is described as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts the afflicted. That gives biblical shape to the request that God would console those harmed by the pray-er’s unkindness.

sections.heading: Teaching me to love with an open heart
sections.text: Father, make my heart larger than my self-protection. Fill me with compassion that overflows toward people in pain, people who lack what they need, and even people who have offended me. Let love be what moves me, not pride, fear, irritation, or convenience. Teach me to live by the way of love because you have loved me first.
theological_themes: Compassion toward the needy and wounded.
Love as the motive and rule of Christian service.
Forgiving and moving toward those who have offended rather than withdrawing in resentment.

scripture_references.connection: John ties Christ’s self-giving love to practical care for brothers and sisters in need. This supports the prayer’s move from feeling compassion to actually giving relief and help.
Paul commands believers to put away bitterness and harshness and to forgive as God forgave them in Christ. That fits the prayer’s request for an open heart toward those who have offended.

sections.heading: Keeping gratitude and humility together
sections.text: God of all grace, make me more thankful and more humble at the same time. I have so many reasons for joy: your patience, your mercy, your daily gifts, and your welcome. But I also have real reasons to be low before you: my sinful nature, the good I have left undone, the chances I have wasted, and the commands I have broken. Give me repentance that leads to life—not regret that only protects my pride, but a turning back to you that you yourself produce.
theological_themes: Gratitude for grace held together with honest humility over sin.
Human unworthiness because of inward corruption, omitted duties, wasted privileges, and disobedience.
Life-giving repentance as God’s gift and work.

scripture_references.connection: Paul distinguishes godly grief that leads to repentance from worldly grief that leads to death. This helps clarify the prayer’s desire for sorrow that turns toward God rather than inward into pride or despair.
Paul says God’s kindness is meant to lead people to repentance. That supports the section’s pairing of gratitude for mercy with humble turning from sin.
Jesus teaches servants not to treat obedience as a ground for boasting. This reinforces the prayer’s humility about service, even when real duties have been performed.

sections.heading: Holding fast to Christ and being sent to serve
sections.text: Bind me more closely to my Lord Jesus. Make my faith cling to him when I am weak and distracted. Make my love for him stronger than my love for comfort, approval, or control. Let his Spirit reach into every part of me—my thoughts, words, habits, desires, and service. Then send me out, not to make much of myself, but to make Christ known to the people around me.
theological_themes: Union with Christ as the source of faithful service.
Faith, love, and the indwelling work of the Holy Spirit shaping the whole person.
Ministry and witness that aim to make Christ known rather than exalt the servant.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes from abiding in him, not from independent effort. This directly supports the request to be bound more closely to Christ before being sent out in service.
Paul prays for believers to be strengthened by the Spirit in the inner person and rooted in Christ’s love. This undergirds the prayer’s desire for Christ’s Spirit to permeate every part of life.
Paul says Christian ministry does not proclaim the minister but Jesus Christ as Lord. That fits the prayer’s final request to be sent out to make Christ known, not to display oneself.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about the 'depravity of my nature' reflects a strongly Augustinian/Reformed account of human sinfulness. I preserved the substance as 'my sinful nature' while avoiding a technical doctrinal label in the prayer text.

The request that God would not withhold mercy because the pray-er withheld mercy from others echoes biblical warnings about unforgiveness and lovelessness, but it can sound as if divine mercy is earned by human mercy. I rendered it as a humble plea for mercy and self-recognition, not a transactional claim.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'bury my sins in the ocean of Jesus’ blood' as an appeal to Christ’s atoning death for forgiveness, and expressed it as guilt being covered and swallowed up in Christ’s mercy.
I treated 'let no evil result' not as a denial of consequences or accountability, but as a plea for God to restrain further harm and heal people damaged by the pray-er’s sin.
I rendered 'the reign of love my motive, the law of love my rule' as love becoming both the inner driver and the practical pattern of service.
I kept the final movement in the original: repentance and humility do not end in self-focus, but in deeper union with Christ and outward witness.
